To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the distribution of errors in dependency parsing are related to the theoretical properties of the parsing models used for learning, that these errors are correlated with the performance of the parser, and that this correlation can be exploited to integrate graph-based and transition-based dependency parsers.

(a) the distribution of parsing mistakes made by data-driven dependency parsers is correlated with theoretical properties, such as the number of arcs and the degree of ambiguity of a sentence, and (b) the integration of a graph-based and transition-based model improves the state of the data-driven dependency parsing.
the distribution of errors is correlated with theoretical properties and that this information can be used to improve accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two questions: (1) How can we use a graph-based dependency parser to improve the accuracy of a transition-based parser?
two questions: (1) how can we exploit the theoretical properties of a parser to improve its performance?

the following questions: 1) How can the theoretical properties of parsing algorithms be used to improve parsing performance? and 2) How can the performance of different algorithms be improved through integration?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the graph-based model is better at handling the long-distance dependencies and the transition-based model at handling the short-distance ones.
the graph-based parser performs better on long distance dependencies and the transition-based parser performs better in the local area.
graph-based models have a tendency to overgenerate, whereas transition-based models have a higher tendency to undergenerate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the graph-based model is more accurate than the transition-based one, but the transition-based model is more robust.
we are able to combine the best features of two models and achieve better results than either model alone.

we have demonstrated that the theoretical properties of dependency parsing models are useful in designing more accurate models, and that it is beneficial to combine models that exploit different types of information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the integration of models can be beneficial, even when the models are based on different theoretical foundations and have different strengths and weaknesses.
by combining models that have different error profiles, the error profile of the combined model can be made closer to an optimal error profile.
the integration of different models can improve parsing performance, even though the models have been trained on different data sets.
